newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ECONOMISTS TRIM SOUTH AFRICAN GROWTH FORECASTS.
newsitem.headline: ECONOMISTS TRIM SOUTH AFRICAN GROWTH FORECASTS.

text.p: Economists have trimmed 1997 growth forecasts for the South African economy after a weak first quarter, but do not expect the country to slide into recession, according to a Reuters survey released on Thursday.

A poll of 31 economists produced a consensus forecast of real gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 2.1 percent, down from 3.1 percent in 1996 and compared to 2.4 forecast at the time of the last quarterly survey in March.
"The economy is slowing but it is not as serious as one might expect just from looking at the first quarter number," said Dave Mohr, chief economist at life assurance giant Old Mutual.
GDP showed a 0.8 percent quarter-on-quarter annualised decline in the first quarter of the year, surprising financial markets and triggering fears of an imminent economic downturn.

But the drop largely reflected a fall in agricultural output after excellent rains in the previous growing season and GDP in the first quarter of 1997 was still nearly 2-1/2 percent higher than in the first quarter of 1996, analysts noted.
Carole Mason, group economist at Investec Bank, said that manufacturing, boosted by exports on the back of a lower rand, would be the key driver of growth in 1997.
"We're still reasonably convinced that there is sufficient buoyancy in the economy on the manufacturing side to ensure positive growth, although it will certainly be lower than last year," she said.
For 1998, the survey forecast a mean growth rate of 3.1 percent, compared to 3.4 forecast in March.

Both the 1997 and 1998 growth forecasts are well below the targets set in the government's five-year Growth, Employment and Redistribution (Gear) strategy, unveiled last June, which envisaged growth of 2.9 percent in 1997 and 3.8 percent in 1998.
South Africa's current account deficit was expected to improve in 1997, helped by stronger exports and reduced domestic demand, the survey showed.

But economists are less bullish than in March, predicting a consensus current account deficit of 5.4 billion rand. That compares to a 1996 deficit of 8.5 but is up from the 3.65 billion forecast for 1997 in March.
The upward revision in the deficit forecast follows a widening in the gap in the first quarter of 1998 to 1.9 billion rand after a negligible 50 million in the last quarter of 1996.
The deterioration in the balance of payments positon in January-March reflected a decline in exports of relatively price-insensitive goods, the fall in the dollar and a lower rand gold price.
The current account deficit was forecast to reach 6.2 billion rand in 1998.
